tagline.text: A 1930s Gaston mansion and the Chapel of the Cartwheels on a Manapla sugar estate

location.label: Location
location.text: Along the Western Nautical Highway, Manapla, Negros Occidental

budget.label: Budget
budget.text: About ₱1,500–2,000 (tour plus lunch per person, 2021 rate)

children.text: Hacienda Rosalia (Hacienda Santa Rosalia) is a compound of the Gaston family's 1930s mansion inside a sugar estate in Manapla. By advance reservation you can tour the two-story house, famous as a film location, and the Chapel of the Cartwheels, and taste estate cooking.

Hacienda Rosalia, also known as Hacienda Santa Rosalia, is a sugar estate in Manapla, in northern Negros Occidental. The Gaston family's mansion and the so-called Chapel of the Cartwheels both stand inside the estate. Wikipedia and similar sources say the estate was founded in 1930 and the mansion built in the 1930s, while a Philstar article and a local culture-festival page date the house to 1935 and 1932 respectively, so the years differ slightly. This guide therefore says simply "the 1930s."

The mansion was built by sugar businessman Jose Gaston. His grandfather, the Frenchman Yves Leopold Gaston, is said to have arrived in the Philippines in 1837, found land suited to sugarcane in Silay around 1840, and brought in an iron mill that opened the way to sugar production for export. Jose's father, Victor Gaston, had the house in Silay that is now the Balay Negrense museum, and the Manapla mansion is described as inspired by that house. Jose and his wife Consuelo had eight children, and Consuelo is said to have designed most of the furniture.

What makes this place appealing is that it is not a museum behind glass cases. You walk, with a guide, through a living house and estate that the family still looks after. Surviving features include wooden furniture in a French Creole style suited to the tropics, solihiya (woven cane) chairs, hand-crocheted bedspreads, and a two-story house with seven balconies. In the garden are a Victorian fountain with two children riding a turtle and a fish, and a huge concrete shoe-shaped house, both great for photos.

The other draw is film. The mansion is widely known as a location for Peque Gallaga's period epic "Oro, Plata, Mata" (sources disagree on the release year, giving 1982 or 1985), and it is also a main location of the 2013 film "Sonata." Keep in mind, though, that it is a private residence, not a sightseeing spot you can enter at any time. Advance reservation is the rule, and you should always confirm just before you go that it is operating.

This is a two-story colonial-style mansion built in the 1930s. The ground floor has a parlor and a large library; upstairs, bedrooms flank the central sala, with the dining room and kitchen at the back. It has as many as seven balconies, and the local hardwood floors and carved stair railings stand out.

This small chapel stands a few meters from the mansion. It is described as using leftover cartwheels in its walls, with a roof shaped like the traditional Filipino hat, the salakot. It is said to have been where estate workers worshipped. It is sometimes under renovation, so ask when you book.

From the tower, which you climb by a narrow staircase, you can see the surrounding sugarcane fields and the chapel below. One guide describes a 360-degree view. The stairs are narrow, so non-slip shoes are a good idea.

In the garden is a concrete shoe-shaped building reminiscent of the Old Woman Who Lived in a Shoe, said to have once been a children's playground. It is a popular photo spot, alongside the Victorian fountain of two children riding a turtle and a fish.

The Philstar article points out where scenes of "Oro, Plata, Mata" were shot, including the party scene in the upstairs sala, the mahjong scene on the balcony, and a scene beside the garden shoe. If you watch the film first, it is great fun to recognize the same balcony and sala.

The grounds include a freshwater pool said to have served as a hiding place in World War II. A garden with flowers, shrubs, palms and herbs, plus a windmill and a basketball court, are also mentioned. A recent visitor reported the pool was empty, so do not expect to swim.

blocks.title: Dining table for 24 and family heirlooms

children.text: The dining room has a large table and cabinets holding silverware, porcelain and crystal. Upstairs are old photographs and handmade linens, and on the entrance table downstairs sits a family tree with descendants' names written in a circle. The table's capacity is given as 18 in one source and 24 in another, so follow the latest explanation on site.

Dishes mentioned include Adobong Milyonaryo, Msgr. GG's pochero, dinuguan with puto Manapla, and sab-a turon, all made with ingredients from the estate. Meals come as a set menu arranged in advance, so if you want to eat, be sure to say so when you book.
Leave your Bacolod hotel by car and head north along the highway (Western Nautical Highway). It is described as about
50 minutes–1 hour
by car from the city, so allow plenty of time.
Pass Victorias City, then follow the sign on the left into a narrow road. Park behind the building and meet the guide you have booked.
Look around the ground-floor parlor and library, then walk through the upstairs sala, bedrooms and balconies with a guide. You can hear about film locations and the family's story.
Go down to the garden to see the fountain and the shoe house, then visit the Chapel of the Cartwheels and the viewing tower.
If you have booked, enjoy the heritage lunch in the mansion's dining room. When mealtime comes, take a break and look out over the garden.
Before leaving, check whether there are souvenir bags or local products, then head back to Bacolod or on to Silay.
The tour and meal are described as possible on the same day, one after the other. The schedule is only an example; follow the schedule you are given when you book.

items.title: Silay combination
items.subtitle: The Gaston family story in two houses

children.text: If you have arrived at Bacolod-Silay Airport, go straight to Manapla by car. It is described as about
30 minutes
by car from the airport.
Tour the mansion at Hacienda Rosalia and stay for lunch.
Move on to Silay town to see old mansions such as the Balay Negrense museum. Check the museum's opening hours locally.
Have dinner in
Silay
and either return to Bacolod or stay the night.
Victor Gaston's house is the Balay Negrense in Silay, and this Manapla mansion is the house of his son Jose. Linking the two connects the family's sugar history in one trip.
Take a direct flight from Manila to Bacolod-Silay Airport (BCD). Flight times and frequencies vary by airline, so check on the booking site.
From the airport to the mansion is about
30 minutes
by car. Use an airport taxi or a pre-booked vehicle.
Take a bus or jeepney bound for Cadiz, Sagay or Escalante from the Bacolod north terminal. Tell the driver you are getting off at Hacienda Santa Rosalia.
One guide says to get off before reaching Manapla town and take a tricycle. The trip is described as taking more than
1 hour
We could not confirm bus fares or frequency. Check locally.

items.title: From Bacolod by car, taxi or van

children.text: It is about
46 minutes–1 hour
by car from Bacolod. Search for Hacienda Santa Rosalia on Google Maps or Waze.
Right after passing Victorias City there is a sign on the left; enter the narrow road and turn left at the T-junction. Parking is behind the building.
In Bacolod you can hire air-conditioned taxis, vans and chartered buses. Negotiate the round-trip waiting fee first.
The road inside the estate is described as partly unpaved and lined with coconut trees. Your shoes may get wet when it rains, so wear comfortable footwear.

Negros is generally known to have a dry season from November to May, which is the best time to travel. Because the visit involves walking the gardens and climbing the tower, a period with little rain is far more comfortable.

The Negros Season of Culture ran from November 4 to December 19 according to a 2020 article, and this mansion was featured as a main attraction. This year's schedule may differ, so check. Visitors say weekday mornings are the quietest.

The highlight of a mansion visit is the estate's food. If you reserve in advance, heritage dishes are served, such as sardine canapés, chorizo cheese diablotin, butter garlic shrimp, Msgr. GG's pochero, dinuguan with puto Manapla, Adobong Milyonaryo and sab-a turon. Drinks mentioned include Rosalia Punch and Sugar Valley Coffee. If you do not reserve, you may not get lunch; one reviewer said they went without a reservation and missed lunch.
It is easier to stay in Bacolod or Silay than at the mansion. There are not many choices near Manapla, so make it a day trip and rest at a hotel in
Bacolod & The Ruins
. There may be roadside eateries nearby, but we could not confirm any, so look locally.
It is a private family home, so be sure to reserve in advance. A phone number and a Facebook page (Hacienda Santa Rosalia) are listed; check the page again for the latest number.
There was information that the Facebook page shows a "closing soon" status. Before you leave, ask whether it is operating and which dates are available.
It is often used as a filming location and may close temporarily. Prepare an alternative in case your plans change.
If you want lunch, say how many people and which menu when you book. There may be a minimum group size.
The rules on photography and drones are unclear. Ask permission before taking photos and do not fly a drone.
Inside the house, do not touch the old furniture and textiles, and follow the guide's explanations.
The tower stairs are narrow. Bring non-slip shoes and travel light.
Weekday mornings are the quietest. If it rains in the afternoon the visit may be cut short, so we recommend arriving in the morning.
Wheelchair access has not been confirmed. Ask when you book if you need it.
This is a privately owned house, not a sightseeing attraction, so you may be turned away without a reservation, and you must confirm whether it is operating and the price before visiting.
A 2021 article and later information differ on the price, so we could not confirm the current amount. Be sure to ask.
Opening hours are sometimes given as 9 a.m. to 5 p.m., but visits are by appointment. Confirm locally.
The mansion and chapel may be under renovation.
If you take the bus, it is easy to miss your stop. Check your position on Google Maps.
In the rainy season the unpaved entrance road may be wet. Check the latest announcements.
A former sugar-aristocrat town on the way from the airport to the mansion. It has the Balay Negrense museum, the Gaston family's Victor house. It is estimated at about
40 minutes
by car; confirm locally.
The central city of Negros Occidental. With hotels and restaurants clustered here, it makes a good base for visiting this mansion.
The ruins of a sugar magnate's mansion that burned down, good for continuing the story of the old sugar era.
The main church of Silay town, a good stop alongside an old-mansion tour.
